topics.text:
There is a game that we play in class called greedy pig here are the rules:

A dice is rolled and the number that shows up is how many points you will get eg i roll and it lands on 6 you get 6 points

You tally up you're points but if it lands on a 2 you lose all you're points and you're out although each turn you have the option to sit down which means you can not stand up again and the points you are left added up is you're score you will keep.

So I came up with a statistical strategy which is the chance of a 2 being rolled each turn is 16.5% so at the fifth or sixth throw you should stand down because the chance a 2 will be rolled is 82.5% and 99% do you have any other strategies?

topics.title: AMC8 2016 number 24
topics.text:
The digits $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, and $5$ are each used once to write a five-digit number $PQRST$. The three-digit number $PQR$ is divisible by $4$, the three-digit number $QRS$ is divisible by $5$, and the three-digit number $RST$ is divisible by $3$. What is $P$?



I have been trying this problems for a long time and then read the solution. However, I was not able to understand the solution. The solution I was reading is posted below.



We see that since $QRS$ is divisible by $5$, $S$ must equal either $0$ or $5$, but it cannot equal $0$, so $S=5$. We notice that since $PQR$ must be even, $R$ must be either $2$ or $4$. However, when $R=2$, we see that $T \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$, which cannot happen because $2$ and $5$ are already used up; so $R=4$. This gives $T \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, meaning $T=3$. Now, we see that $Q$ could be either $1$ or $2$, but $14$ is not divisible by $4$, but $24$ is. This means that $R=4$ and $P=\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 1}$



The part that I was not able to understand was when the solution started using mods.



Thanks,

Mathprogidy

topics.title: Fun Geometry Problem
topics.text:
What is the ratio (from least to greatest) of two triangles areas who have side lengths of 18-24-30 and 14-48-50?



SolutionThese are just two Pythagorean triples in disguise.  18-24-30 is just the 3-4-5 multiplied by 6. 14-48-50 is just the 7-24-25 multiplied by 2.  So now lets find these areas.  Since 30 is the longest side 30 would be the hypotenuse.  So the base and height would be 18 and 24.  Using the formula to find the area of a triangle: $\frac{\text{base}\cdot \text{height}}{2}$ we can substitute base and height for 18 and 24 to get $\frac{18 \cdot 24}{2}=216$ so the area of the first triangle is 216.  We can do the same fore the 14-48-50 triangle.  Since 50 is the longest side it is the hypotenuse.  Therefore the sides 14 and 48 are the base and the height.  Now we have $\frac{14 \cdot 48}{2}=336$ so the area of the second triangle.  So the ratio of areas from least to greatest is $216 : 336$.

topics.title: Geometric sequence in triangle side lengths
topics.text:
I'm stuck on Problem 1.661 from Competition Math for Middle School by J. Batterson, which is to find the perimeter of the smallest triangle whose integer side lengths form a geometric sequence whose common ratio r is not equal to 1.  The solution provided is a guess-and-check solution, and I'd like to know if there is a solution that doesn't involve guess-and-check.  My work so farLet $a$, $ar$, and $ar^2$ be the lengths of the triangle (r is the common ratio).  By the triangle inequality, $a+ar>ar^2$, $a+ar^2>ar$, and $ar+ar^2>a$.  Since $a+ar>ar^2$, $a(1+r)>ar^2$.  a>0 (since it is a side length of a triangle), so we do not need to worry about dividing by 0 or having to flip the inequality sign when dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number when both sides of $a(1+r)>ar^2$ are divided by $a$.  We have $1+r>r^2$.  Rearranging the terms, we get $r^2<r+1$.  Setting the right side of the inequality to 0, we have $r^2-r-1<0$.  Multiplying by 4, we have $4r^2-4r-4<0$, and adding 5 to both sides we have $4r^2-4r+1<5$, or $(2r-1)^2<5$.  Thus $-\sqrt{5}<2r-1<\sqrt{5}$.  Since $-\sqrt{5}<2r-1$, $\frac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}<r$, but this is obvious since  $\frac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}<0$, and r must be positive (otherwise at least one of the triangle's sides would have to be negative).  $2r-1<\sqrt{5}$, so $r<\frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{2}$.  $a+ar^2>ar$, so $a(1+r^2)>ar$, and by the same argument as before, we can divide both sides by a without having to worry about dividing by 0 or having  to flip the inequality sign when dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number.  Thus $1+r^2>r$.  Subtracting r from both sides and rearranging the terms, we get $r^2-r+1>0$.  Multiplying both sides by 4 we have $4r^2-4r+4>0$.  Subtracting 3 from both sides, we have $4r^2-4r+1>-3$, or   $(2r-1)^2>-3$, but this is true for any real r.  $ar+ar^2>a$, so $a(r+r^2)>a$, and $r+r^2>1$.  Subtracting 1 from both sides and rearranging the terms, we have $r^2+r-1>0$.  Multiplying both sides by 4, we have $4r^2+4r-4>0$.  Adding 5 to both sides, we have $4r^2+4r+1>5$, or $(2r+1)^2>5$.  Thus, $2r+1<-\sqrt{5}$ or $2r+1>\sqrt{5}$,  If $2r+1<-\sqrt{5}$, $r<\frac{-\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$, but r is positive, so $2r+1>\sqrt{5}$, and $r>\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$.  We have        $r<\frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{2}$ and $r>\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$, so $\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}<r<\frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{2}$.


I don't know what to do next.  Is there a solution without guess-and-check?  If so, please tell me what it is, because I haven't found a solution without guess-and-check.

topics.title: Easy proof for sum of factors formula.
topics.text:
Recall (if you can (no offense)) the formula for the number of factors (add one to every exponent of the prime factorization Andy multiply). The formula for the number of factors takes advantage of the fact that every single factor is a permutation of the product of the others. The proof for the sum of factors will also use this.



Say there is a number $a$ whose prime factorization was $b^cd^e.........$ Now, we want an expression that gives the sum of the factors. Because each factor is a permutation of the product of all of them, we will make an expression such that every term is a permutation of all the others. Let's start out with the first factor, $b$. We want all the powers of b in one factor. So $b^0 + b + .... + b^c$ is one factor. Now we want all of these powers to be multiplied by the next prime, say $d$. So we basically want all the permutations created from all the powers of $b$ and $d$ and the rest. Let's just focus on b and d. Clearly by now, you can see the expression that gives all the permutations is the one I stated above multiplied by the same expression but $b$ is replaced by $d$. If you apply this logic to all the other factors then you get the sum of factors formula.
